title: A Girl Who Called the Forest Her Bank
text: Have you ever seen a bank with no doors, no guards, and no money? Meet Suryamani, a girl from Jharkhand. When she was a little girl, she didn't play in a park or go to a mall. Her playground was a massive, dark green forest. In fact, she called the forest her 'Sajha Bank' (Shared Bank). But how can a forest filled with trees and animals be a bank? Let's find out!

title: What If the Forest Disappeared?
text: Imagine for a moment: What would happen if all the forests around us suddenly vanished? Where would the birds build their nests? Where would the tigers hide? And what would happen to the people who depend on the forest for their food and medicine? Take a moment to think.

content.title: The Forest Ecosystem
content.description: Notice how every living thing is connected in this invisible web. The trees provide shelter and food, the animals help spread seeds, and the humans protect the forest.

title: The Adivasis: People of the Forest
text: The secret to Suryamani's 'bank' is that forests provide everything her people need: food, medicines, materials to build homes, and even plates made from leaves! People who live in the forest and depend on it are called Adivasis. They take from the forest only what they need, just like taking money from a bank, but they never destroy it. Suryamani speaks the Kuduk language, where 'Torang' means jungle.

content.definition: Original inhabitants or tribal people who live close to nature and depend on forests for their livelihood. (Root: 'Adi' meaning original, 'vasi' meaning dweller)
A word in the Kuduk language that means 'Jungle' or 'Forest'.

title: Your Daily Life vs. Forest Life
text: Reflect on this: You get your vegetables from a supermarket, water from a tap, and medicines from a pharmacy. If you lived in the forest like Suryamani, you would gather wild herbs for medicine and fetch water from a stream. How would your daily routine change? Would you feel more connected to nature?

title: Connecting to Our World
text: Suryamani's story isn't just about one girl. It connects to the Geography of Jharkhand and the Right to Forest Act (2007), which states that people living in forests for at least 25 years have a right over the forest land and what grows on it. In Science, this connects to the Food Web and Photosynthesis—showing how forests are the 'lungs' of our Earth.

content.title: Understanding the Law
content.text: Remind students that the Right to Forest Act (2007) is a crucial real-world law that protects the Adivasis from being unfairly evicted from their ancestral lands.

content.title: Misconception About Adivasis
content.text: Many students think Adivasis harm the forest by cutting trees. The truth is the opposite! Adivasis protect the forests because it is their home and their livelihood.

content.title: The Forest Detective Challenge
content.description: Look around your house right now and find at least 3 items that came directly from a forest (e.g., wooden furniture, paper, a rubber eraser, or spices like cinnamon). Create a mini-presentation to explain how these items travelled from a forest to your home!
